Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, in these the closing moments of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I wish to address the house from the standpoint of a business man. As a business man I am obliged from time to time to supervise advertising matter and to write letters, and I always endeavour to approach my subject and to present my thoughts in such a way that the one whom I am addressing will understand what I am placing before him. Particularly have I in mind my own business.
We are gathered here from all parts of Canada to deal with important national questions, and our criticisms should be constructive and our policies advanced in such a way that they will be understood by the public. But I have sometimes wondered, as I have sat here since the opening of parliament, whether the messages which have gone forth from this house from those taking part in this debate, on the government side and from the opposition and the two other groups represented in this chamber, were calculated to bring about the best results from the standpoint of the nation. Are they going to have a good or a harmful effect upon our citizens as a whole? Are they going to help mould the lives of our youth so that they will be better citizens of the future to occupy the seats we are endeavouring to fill here? I wonder also what has been the effect upon the average mature mind of the messages which have been broadcast from this house, through the press and by other means, as to our willingness to cooperate with the government in bringing about those results which are so much to be desired, conditions being as they are in this country to-day.
I sat and pondered this question, Mr. Speaker, and I was impressed by the thought which the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) brought before parliament, a thought which, I believe, is in the minds of

The Address-Mr. Isnor
many. Are we here to fight one another in regard to policies, or are we here to cooperate in offering constructive criticism and constructive policies which will be helpful to the government, instead of doing as has been done so often-I say this with all due respect for the views held by the various groups in this house-unfairly criticizing, apparently with the one thought in mind of obstructing the various measures brought forward by the government? I believe the thought expressed by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce is in the minds of a great many people throughout Canada. I do not wish to compliment her particularly upon her speech; but I do think she was talking good common sense, and it is common sense that is going to help Canada to prosper and bring about a return to better days. If we use common sense, instead of offering unfair criticisms, I believe our efforts will be better appreciated by the people outside this house.
I was also impressed by a statement I saw in the newspapers, credited to one of the veteran members of this house, that he did not think the country desired this continual repetition of compliments paid by the various speakers to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I sincerely trust the hon. members will not misunderstand me or think I am lacking in courtesy, but it does appear to me that it would be sufficient if the giving of the compliments usually paid to the mover and the seconder were restricted to the leaders of the various parties-the leader of the government, the leader of the opposition, and the leaders of the other two groups, or their representatives. I think that would be quite sufficient to bring to the attention of the people that the speeches of the mover and seconder were appreciated. On the other hand I think it is only fair that the mover (Mr. Matthews) and seconder (Mr. Chevrier) should know that we, the other hon. members, appreciate the time and thought they put into their addresses and that our compliments are extended to them in all sincerity. I think that is all I need to say on that subject, or members will begin to think I am like some others and the country perhaps feel that this is just another collection of words, but I thought it was necessary to put these views before the house. I am satisfied at least that I am reflecting the views honestly held by many outside parliament as to our methods of carrying on the nation's business.
I always hesitate, Mr. Speaker, to advance views held by any particular section of our nation; for I realize, whether it be a question of tariffs or taxes or social measures or a trade agreement, that the nation as a whole
must be considered. We are gathered here, not as representatives of any particular section only, but as representing also Canada as a whole from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and our suggestions offered in good faith and sincerely and honestly may be helpful in bringing about a solution of our problems.
Coming as I do from the maritimes I listened with deep interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and to the views expressed by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. McAvity), who very frankly and, may I add, very fairly, put before the house problems affecting particularly the eastern maritimes. I, sir, wish to bring before the house certain matters pertaining to the eastern maritimes, and perhaps more especially the province of Nova Scotia, with a view to something helpful being done for that particular section of the country.
I should also like to make mention of the able address we heard this afternoon from the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier). The hon. member is well acquainted with the fishing industry of our province and well versed as to the needs of the fishermen. He is therefore well able to speak with authority on that subject, and when one so well qualified to speak addresses the house on the needs he knows so well, I think the government would be well advised to take his suggestions into careful Consideration.
We from the maritimes, and particularly from Nova Scotia, do not perhaps press our claims as strongly upon the government as do members from other sections of Canada. Listening to the discussions in the house from year to year we cannot help but be impressed by the manner in which western members advance the claims of that section of the country. Perhaps it is because we are a little backward in the extreme east that we do not press our claims as strongly; but we have in the east pressing problems which affect our fishermen, farmers, miners, and lumbering interests in Nova Scotia, and which are, I am pleased to say, receiving the attention of the government. I have in mind, for instance, the trade agreement which was recently concluded with the United States, but I propose to speak of that at a later date.
I was especially pleased to note that the speech from the throne made reference to a matter that is of great importance to our section of the country. I refer to the West Indies trade treaty. As is mentioned in the speech from the throne, notice has already been given, effective December 31, 1939, terminating this agreement. I feel it is proper that views
The Address-Mr. Isnor

held in connection with such an important matter should be made known to the government, so I am venturing to touch upon it at the present time.
Trade with the West Indies is of vital importance to the eastern maritimes, especially to the port of Halifax. Halifax merchants for many generations have been actively engaged in this particlar trade, and they know what is needed to further its development. I remember that in 1924 certain definite recommendations were made to the government of that time. An exceptionally strong committee, composed of men who had been engaged for years in the trade between Halifax port and the West Indies, was appointed by the Halifax board of trade to go into this matter, and they did so very thoroughly. Not only did they gather data from our own province and the adjoining provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, but they sought to find out what effects such a trade would have on the rest of Canada, and they compiled and forwarded to the government recommendations which, I think, if they had been carried out would have been of material benefit to our province, to the maritimes in the east and to the whole of Canada.
It is with this fact in mind that I make this suggestion to the government, and particularly to our own minister, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley), whom we in the maritimes hold in very high regard. We can approach him in a spirit of brotherhood as one who knows our problems and who is always willing and ready to cooperate with us in regard to them. We sincerely hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), when the time arrives to discuss the details of such an agreement, will call into consultation men from Halifax who have an intimate knowledge of the trade requirements and the relations between Canada and the West Indies. I might say that the report of the committee I have mentioned was unanimously approved by the council of the Halifax board of trade and also by the council of the Saint John board of trade. We are agreed in regard to the requirements so far as the maritimes are concerned.
This matter touches us from the viewpoint of the potato market, whose needs were so well placed before the house a few days ago by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Douglas). He pointed out the advantages of the market not only in the West Indies but in Cuba. I could also mention the advantages, from the fishermen's standpoint, of a trade agreement. These two considerations in particular should receive careful attention by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I stress especially the

importance of having persons familiar with the trade situation sit in with the government in discussing the details.
Another question, which concerns equally the maritimes and the progress the maritimes must make if they are to advance as we hope they will, is that of transportation. I was pleased the other evening, to hear the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) allude to the promise made at the time of confederation with regard to our railway system. Coming as it did from an Ontario member, the remark showed the proper spirit. I feel that we should have a complete link from the Atlantic to the Pacific serving us in the maritimes in such a way as to permit us to place our goods in the eastern and central markets quickly enough to enjoy a profitable business. We can do that only if we are provided with a transportation system sufficiently rapid to enable us to place our products in a good state of preservation on the central market. I have in mind, of course, that important commodity, fish. I would ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) to give this question his careful attention.
I realize that I must touch carefully on the subject of transportation. Its pros and cons are being discussed by the best brains of the country. The biggest men in the transportation business are making radio speeches and sending broadcasts of printed speeches as regards amalgamation, some advocating it, some opposing it. We in the maritimes look on the question of amalgamation in what is perhaps a rather distinctive way. We know it was a vital instrument in connection with the confederation pact. We realize that there are deficits from year to year, but we also realize the high position in which the Canadian National railways stands to-day. That remark may be subject to criticism, but I would make a comparison of the various railways in order to justify my position. The justification lies in the relation of the railway deficits to the amount of new national wealth and national income available through the carrying of the railways into different parts of Canada. It is not only the private capital invested in the railways which is to be considered; it is not solely a matter of profit upon expenditure for railways or the actual earnings of the capital structure, but rather the increased wealth which is derived from the advancing of transportation facilities into sections which have not as yet been fully developed.
The vast bulk of goods for internal and external trade is moved by railway, and no other form of transportation in existence or

The Address-Mr. Isnor
in prospect is physically capable of handling the tonnage. Trucks have taken profitable short-haul package freight from the railways, leaving them carrying long-haul bulk commodities on which the business and the very existence of the country depends, and at rates so low that the carriage constitutes a subsidy to the business interests. That the present rate structure will not permit a return on railway investments is shown by the fact that in the first six months of 1938 eighty-six per cent of the railways of the United States failed to meet their fixed charges. In 1938 the United States railways failed to meet fixed charges by $125,000,000, and a total of 111 companies, including thirty-nine class A roads, were in receivership. That is a matter which should receive the careful attention of those who are so ready to criticize the earnings of the Canadian National Railways. This was all under private ownership, because private interests control the railways in the United States. We are in a somewhat different position. In Canada, along with the private railway system, we have our publicly owned railways. In Canada, with a much smaller population per mile and a more rigorous climate, it is obvious that the increasing failure of railways under private ownership to meet fixed charges will become more pronounced as time goes on. It would appear that the day of fat dividends in railways is over.
Let me ask:	Are the troubles of the Canadian Pacific Railway caused by these general conditions, or is their spokesman right in blaming the government-owned Canadian National Railways. As regards the statement that great savings could be made and dividend payments resumed through amalgamation and the abandonment of certain railway mileage, it would seem that the resumption of dividend payments is increasingly remote, because private ownership cannot accomplish this elsewhere, as is shown by the facts I have already quoted in connection with the United States roads. The argument in regard to large savings was not substantiated before the senate inquiry last year.
I place these facts before the house so that hon. members will not be so ready to criticize unfairly our own Canadian National Railways. In the United States the abandonment of railway mileage not paying fixed charges has invariably resulted in a short time in wholesale business bankruptcy, a serious fall in property values and a loss of population in the communities affected, which did not oppose abandonment. The abandonment of certain lines in the United States was not opposed, and the tearing up of rails that took place
was generally followed by a depression in business and a fall in property values. I suggest, therefore, that before the abandonment of lines is seriously considered this fact be borne in mind. The abandonment of lines in the United States was, in nearly every instance, the result of advances made by truck transportation, and we are facing the same situation in Canada to-day. Our roads are being honeycombed by trucks carrying freight in competition with the railways, taking the profitable business and leaving the very necessary long haul for the railways.
It is to be noted that in 1920 the privately owned roads of which the Canadian National railway system is composed had, under private ownership, a total operating deficit of $35,000,000, not to mention those which had defaulted on capital investment. From 1923 there has never been an operating deficit under government ownership; on the contrary, there have been operating profits totalling in excess of $360,000,000.
To any one who examines the monthly and yearly statistics set out under various headings for comparison of operations of railways in Canada, the United States and other countries, it is evident that the Canadian National Railways ranks with the best. Propaganda to the contrary cannot be supported by facts. Statements are frequently made in regard to the yearly deficit of the Canadian National Railways, and this, I would point out, is caused, as I believe all will appreciate, largely by interest charges on the capital investment of the former privately owned companies which were taken over under the one management.
In the United States and elsewhere, continued failure to meet fixed charges has resulted in bankruptcy and receivership, the capital structure being written down to a figure consonant with the operating revenues, and the original investors taking the loss. I need not point out that if this had been done in Canada the financial structure of the Canadian National Railways would appear in an altogether different light to-day. It would have been a great deal better for our country and we should have had a truer picture. I would suggest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) that though he has made advances-two years ago he did make advances in connection with the financial set-up, which were carried into effect last year-he should go still further and write off wherever possible. It is true that there are some capital investments which cannot be written off; but he could go a long way further in this
The Address-Mr. Isnor

direction, so that the general public would have a truer reflection of the actual workings of the Canadian National Railways.
It was decided, rightly or wrongly, not to do this in the case of the privately owned systems of the Canadian National Railways. Whether that was justified; whether it was done to save privately owned investments, I am not in a position to say. Operating revenues do not meet similar overhead charges on other roads and cannot have done so in the case of the Canadian National Railways, with the result that the deficit on capital investment is piling up and is being compounded. I might speak at some length on the compounding of deficits caused by increasing deficits in the capital structure, but I shall not discuss that question now. The advocates of amalgamation have offered no solution of this problem of capital investment indebtedness. On the contrary it would appear that they naively expect the government to retain these obligations and hand over the very considerable operating earnings of the system to the proposed amalgamated management. Can it be that they also expect the government to take over the capital investment obligations of the Canadian Pacific Railway without a writing down and without even the prospect of getting any of the operating surplus? Can propaganda, however dressed up, put over such a scheme? If it does, though I do not think it can, it will at least have trouble in convincing anyone with ordinary sense that this scheme will do otherwise than further embarrass the government and increase its obligations, and it will afford relief to no one except the holders of Canadian Pacific railway bonds and stocks.
In conclusion, with respect to the railway question, I would point out that it is estimated that for each dollar invested in railway construction in Canada there has been created ten dollars of national capital wealth. The efficiency of the Canadian National Railways has steadily and progressively been bettered under government management. It now stands in the front rank. Its property and equipment have been well maintained, and it is in an excellent position to take full advantage of increase in the volume of traffic. For instance, last fall business conditions turned upward, with a marked increase in traffic, and net revenue for October amounted to $4,650,000, the largest for any month since 1029, showing that there is nothing lacking in the operating efficiency of this system. The ability to respond so quickly to increased traffic gives an indication of the potential earning power of the Canadian National Railways.

Hon. members may wonder why I give this background of the Canadian National Railways. I am interested because the port of Halifax is the eastern terminus of that railway system. I am interested to see as much traffic as possible go through our Atlantic ports. I feel that with the Canadian National making such a good showing as far as its Canadian lines are concerned, the Minister of Transport would be well advised to consider seriously doing away with the existing lines of the Canadian National in the United States. I have particularly in mind doing away with the terminal at Portland. I would advocate this even if these lines showed a substantial surplus of earnings; but I am reliably advised that such is not the case, that on the contrary they show a decided deficit. In view of this and the urgent need of employment for our waterfront workers, stevedores and men who handle railway freight, I would urge the Minister of Transport to give this suggestion very careful consideration. Why should we ship our goods through United States ports? There should be no need for doing so when we have such excellent ports as Saint John and particularly Halifax. So I leave that suggestion with the Minister of Transport, confident of his capacity to make it a reality. I hope to see railways, steamship lines and airways, and, I trust, later, highway transport, all under his direction. He should not feel satisfied until he has linked the Atlantic with the Pacific by a transportation system that will be satisfactory to every section of our country.
I should like to have touched on the recently consummated trade agreement between Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom, and the benefits accruing to the eastern maritimes particularly in respect to fish, potatoes and lumber, and even apples, because I believe that one goes with the other. While there is no direct increased benefit for the apple grower under the recent trade treaty, the advantages gained in respect to fish and lumber will go a long way to help us by creating additional trade which will be extremely beneficial to our section of the dominion.
I should like also to have gone into the question of defence in relation to the Atlantic, but there will be opportunity for that when the defence estimates are before us. I feel I should not sit down without expressing appreciation to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) on behalf of those living on the Atlantic coast for so generously considering that part of the country. Our defences were sadly lacking. We have de-

The Address-Mr. Manion
fences, perhaps better than a good many are aware, but they need to be brought up to date. I am pleased to note in the estimates that a sufficiently large sum has been made available, and I feel sure that our Atlantic coast will be put in a position at least to help defend the rest of Canada, if necessary, although I hope that necessity will never arise.
How any thinking member, in the face of the many important matters mentioned in the speech from the throne, can rise in his place and talk about the speech not containing anything worth while is beyond me. Instead of finding fault it would be better to listen and read and pick from the speeches of those who have endeavoured to offer constructive thoughts, the ideas which, when put together, would lead to a brighter and better Canada.
In conclusion, may I say that the views represented in parliament by the various groups simply reflect a cross section of nation-wide opinion. We are no different from what we were when elected in 1935; we are just human, striving to carry out our duties honestly and sincerely. We are no worse-no better perhaps -than those who are using the radio and newspapers to tear down without a plan of rebuilding. The public listen, smile, and say, "Yes, there is a lot of truth in what that fellow says, but why does he not give us a complete plan and specifications by which to build a stronger Canadian structure?" Would it not be far better if radio critics and others would unite in bringing out the good things about our Canada, following the line recently adopted by Canadian Industries Limited in a recent newspaper advertisement, which reads:
" The brightest spot on earth."
The start of another year is a good time for stock-taking, and when we do it on a national scale we see that Canada is literally "the brightest spot on earth."
Many things have contributed to Canada's progress. Nature put vast oceans to the east and west of us and history placed a friendly neighbour on the south. History also tells us that our forefathers were rugged men, capable of enduring the hardships of founding a new homeland. Experience, passed on to us from those pioneers of our two great races, has helped give us courage and determination to carry on against every obstacle. Back of all this we have supplies of natural resources which are the envy of all.
We have these things, and yet, perhaps we are too close to them. We take for granted those things which look so priceless to the outsider, when, if we will but believe it, we have "the brightest spot on earth" for our home-Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I must apologize for taking up any more time of the house at this stage, but
since there is plenty of time for the vote this evening there is one subject with which I wish to deal briefly; not because it is my desire to speak again, but because of an attack made upon me in this house by an hon. member of the Liberal party, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank). Before dealing with that subject, however, I wish to say that after an absence of three years I have been pleased generally with the conduct of the debate. Practically all hon. members have spoken on a reasonably high plane. That is as it should be. I believe that as far as we are able we should avoid misstating facts, falsifying the record, or anything of that sort. We may misinterpret each other's acts; I may attack my right hon. friend upon interpretation I put on some of his acts, but I shall at all .times avoid misrepresenting anything he has done.
May I at the same time thank hon. members of all parties and all sections of the house for the kindly reception they have given me upon my return to the house, and the kind words so many have spoken of me. There are, however, always one or two, even in small groups, who cannot avoid flinging mud. Let me say now that I have no intention at any time of permitting anyone to fling mud at me, in the hope that some of it may stick. I will correct such statements on every occasion, no matter who the hon. member may be who makes them.
The hon. gentleman to whom I refer, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, made some charges against me, and if I were guilty of them I would not be fit to sit as a member of this house. In order that I may not be accused of misquoting him I shall read his words. Speaking of myself, he said:
He was Minister of Railways during those five years, and during those years the Canadian National Railways were systematically sabotaged.
A little further on he said:
I draw the inference from his conduct as Minister of Railways that the systematic sabotaging of the railway that went on during those years was largely attributable to him.
I contradicted that and said:
That statement is absolutely untrue. There was no sabotaging of the Canadian National Railways at any time.
Mr. Maybank: It was sabotaged from the day the late government came into office until the day it went out.
Mr. Manion: That is not true.
A little further on he said:
But from the moment he took over that portfolio-
Speaking again of myself.
-the manner of carrying on the business of the railroad was changed. We know that the
The Address-Mr. Manion

men who were working for the railway during those five years were trembling every day that he went to his office as Minister of Railways. Certainly what I said in regard to telegraph and express business is true, and in the light of that it is a reasonable inference to draw that this was the first step towards complete amalgamation.
Those are some of the statements the hon. gentleman made about myself, and of course I use the expression "honourable gentleman" in a parliamentary sense.

speechtext: Easy; he is not here.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not here; but he did not know whether I was going to be in the house when he attacked me so violently, misstating facts and accusing me of doing things which, as I said, would not be done by anyone worthy to sit in this house. If any man within or without this house, any Canadian, wilfully sabotaged the Canadian National Railways he would not be fit to bear the name Canadian. I say that here to-night.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: But not my hon. friend. It was a charge against the previous government.

Oh, no. I read the words and I do not wish to read them again. If the right hon. gentleman will look up what I read from the speech of the hon. member, he will see that the whole blame was placed on my shoulders. If, however, that were all, perhaps I should not mind so much; but since the hon. gentleman spoke in this house and made that charge-that false charge-it has been spread across this country by means of the radio. In addition to that, other charges of a like nature were made against me during the campaign in London. I was charged with the same thing. I was accused of closing the shops of the Canadian National; I was charged, as the hon. gentleman charged me, with trying to force the amalgamation of the railways, and I was accused of crucifying Sir Henry Thornton. The campaign carried on against me there was the most vicious one in which I have ever taken part, and I have been in quite a number. Let me give the house one illustration. In the railway station at London there is a plaque in honour of Sir Henry Thornton. Two or three nights before the election there was a religious ceremony held beneath that plaque, and I have before me

a statement which was made at that time by a gentleman who, I suppose, from his standpoint, spoke in good faith.

speechtext: If I may interrupt fQr a moment, I hope my hon. friend will make it clear, before he begins to quote what may have been said by different persons who participated in that campaign, that he had no Liberal opponent in that by-election. So I assume they were not Liberal speakers.

speechtext: Quite. I am sorry I did not say that; I took it for granted that everyone was aware of the fact that I had no Liberal opponent. I have already thanked the right hon. gentleman and his party for their courteous treatment of me at that time. I do not wish to get into anything controversial, but these charges all link up in the same way. I am referring now to the charges that were made by the supporters of the candidate who ran against me in London.

speechtext: What party?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. This is what was said by the gentleman who, so far as I remember, spoke at the so-called religious ceremony:
Yet in spite of all the late Sir Henry did for the C.N.R., for Canada and for the British empire, he was crucified for no other reason than he was too progressive.
Of course anybody who knows anything realizes that the "religious" ceremony was a sacrilege; that it was put on not for religious purposes but absolutely for the purpose of playing politics. And that was only part of it. At that time not only was I charged with all the crimes of which I was accused by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre; I was charged with opposing old age pensions, unemployment insurance, the organization of bank employees, and, in fact, all social legislation. And I say here to-night that every one of those charges, without exception, was just as false as was the charge made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre against me with regard to sabotaging the Canadian National Railways. The object, of course, is clear to anyone. The object was to capture the labour and Canadian National railway votes in big railway centres. London is a big railway centre; so is Winnipeg, and there are others as well. So, since these arguments no doubt will be used on other occasions, I intend to put the true story on the record. I hope it will not take very long; and then if others make statements against me that are false, at any rate I shall know the term that should be applied to them, even if I cannot use it in this house.

The Address-Mr. Manion
Tlie reply I desire to make deals merely with the facts. I want to say again, sir, what I have said in other places, that I am prouder of the work I did for the Canadian National Railways between 1930 and 1935 than of anything else I have done during the twenty years I have been in public life. Far from attempting to sabotage the Canadian National Railways, we did much to help them, and I will prove that. Sabotaging means wrecking. What kind of Canadian could he be who would attempt to wreck the Canadian National, owned by the government of Canada, which means by us? It is our railway. To my mind an attempt to sabotage that railway would be both disloyal and unpatriotic; and I repeat that it could be done only by a man who would be unworthy to sit in this house.
The Canadian Pacific is also a great Canadian institution, and certainly I do not think any hon. member who merits the word "honourable" before his name would think of intentionally damaging either of these two great railway companies. What I did for the Canadian National Railways, or at any rate what I as minister helped to do, was to put the Canadian National in an economic operating condition, and I shall endeavour to prove that. Indeed, I think I can bring that proof from the mouths of the Canadian National officers themselves. Mr. Fairweather appeared before the senate railway committee last year and was in the witness box for over a day. In number 7 of the proceedings before that committee, Mr. Fairweather is reported as follows:
When the depression hit us we started to reduce expenses everywhere we could find them, and we did reduce expenses to such an extent that in 1937 we handled the same gross revenue with $20,000,000 less of operating expenses.
I think that is sufficient proof. In the evidence before that committee a number of statistics were cited, and the actual figures are given in regard to the cost of operating the road, and the returns. I should like to put those figures on record. In 1931 the income of the whole Canadian National system was, in round figures, a little over $200000,000. In 1937, six years later, the income was $198,000,000 odd. The two figures are so close that Mr. Fairweather made the statement that the income was the same in those two years. Then, the expenses in 1931 were $199,000,000, and in 1937, $180,000,000 a difference really not of $20,000,000, as Mr. Fair-weather states, but of $19,000,000. After all, sir, that surely is absolute proof that the economies I frankly admit of forcing upon the Canadian National Railways were necessary. The fact that they could do the same
business in 1937 as in 1931 for $19,000,000 less surely shows that there were wild extravagances-those are words I have often used- in the handling of the Canadian National Railways when we came into power in 1930. That to me is a justification of our whole position.
There is a deficit this year which may amount to $50,000,000. Instead of that deficit of $50,000,000 there would have been that other $19,000,000 more, or roughly $70,000,000. The railway question to-day is a serious one in this country. Everybody realizes this, and people are realizing it more and more. There has been a great campaign carried on for the unification of the railways. The greater the deficit, the greater the feeling among business men particularly that something must be done with these railways. So that in correcting those extravagances and in bringing down legitimately the expenses of the Canadian National Railways-we started it, and my hon. friends are carrying it on; I am not suggesting anything to the contrary- those who did it were the real friends of the Canadian National Railways. We were not saboteurs-if that is the proper word-but we were friends of the Canadian National Railways.
I am not going to discuss the railways in detail, but the reason the railways are in difficulties to-day is very clear. First, there was a great deal of over-building. Second-and this is the big question to-day, the main reason for the present difficulties of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway is that automobiles came into competition. There was the expansion of the automobile industry to contend with. We have the fact that large numbers of people are to-day travelling in automobiles rather than on the railways. Again, much of the freight for short hauls is carried by trucks.
I am going to mention at this point-and I have the information in the same lot of tables-a startling fact which struck me when I was reading the evidence last year with respect to the Canadian National Railways. I refer to the figures respecting the numbers of passengers carried. I hold in my hand a document showing the figures which were given before the senate committee. They are startling figures and to a large extent show the reason why the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway are encountering a great deal of difficulty to-day in financing. In 1923 the passengers carried by the two railways numbered 38,000,000. In 1937 there were only 18,000,000, or less than half the number carried in the earlier year.
The Address-Mr. Manion

That to a large extent is the answer to the troubles of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways and, indeed, to the troubles of all the railways on this continent. I say that because the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific most certainly are not the only railways on the continent which have had their troubles. A book I picked up the other day showed the figures for the United States. I have reference to the magazine called Time published in the United States. The figures therein quoted show that the United States railways in 1922-just one year before the figures I have cited for Canada-carried a total of 537,000,000 passengers, while in 1937 they carried 251,000,000. Again we have a figure which is less than half, or the same proportion exactly as were carried by the Canadian railways.
That answers, largely, the whole trouble of the railways on this continent. Figures in the same table show the interesting fact that the freight carried on the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways was less in 1937 than it was in 1923. This, is an extraordinary fact, considering that the country has developed somewhat, but nevertheless clearly indicates the reasons why the railways are in difficulties.
So far as sabotage is concerned, I deny it absolutely and unequivocally; I resent very much the suggestion by anybody-and it is made so far as I know by only one man of all the speakers, and there were over one hundred of them-and I resent the charge very much. I hope that all lion, members even for political reasons, will not descend to that depth of attack in the future.
In regard to jobs, I was accused by the same hon. member-I read the statement a moment ago and it is unnecessary to read it again-that so long as I was Minister of Railways no Canadian National Railways employee could come to the office in the morning without wondering if he would have a job in the department. I had nothing to do, in any shape or form, with the job of anybody in the Canadian National Railways. It was entirely the management which looked after that. I am sure the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) will say the situation is the same to-day, and I shall believe him if he says so. The jobs in the Canadian National Railways are entirely in the hands of the management. Then, why charge me with taking away the jobs of men on the road? There was a depression which started in 1929 and which continued downward until 1933. During that time large numbers of men were laid off from the service of both roads. But this had nothing to do with me. I never interfered in any manner or form with the employees of the Canadian National Railways. I had no power to do so.
[Mi* Manion.]
I would probably have been told by the management to attend to my own business, and rightly.
Twice when we were in power I tried to get a favour from the Canadian National management. I mention these instances, because they were the only exceptions. One had reference to a doctor in the west-I shall not give his name or the place from which he comes. But he was a friend of many years, and a Liberal in politics. A certain organization, which had no right to interfere in the Canadian National Railways, attempted to have this man laid off. When we first came into power Sir Henry Thornton came to me and told me that this organization was trying to get this man dismissed, with which action he did not agree. He said, "What is your feeling?" and I backed him up. I knew the man, personally. He had gone to school with me. I had a personal friendship for him, and I have yet. Sir Henry felt the same way, and the man was kept on. But when Sir Henry Thornton left and we appointed the late Judge Fullerton as chairman of the board, one of his first acts was to dismiss this man. I protested. Without my knowledge, Mr. Bennett, who knew the man, because he had come from his section of the country, made similar protests in connection with what he, too, considered an unjust dismissal. This man had been a life-long Liberal and had oome from a Liberal family. We both protested, but we did not succeed in having the man retained, and he has been out of a job ever since.
The only other interference I ever attempted was with respect to a man who came from the constituency of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), namely, that of Port Arthur. This man was a watchman who had been laid off because of age. A number of his friends approached me at the time, as minister. Every hon. member coming from a railway constituency has no doubt had a similar experience. Probably the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. McKinnon) -has sometimes done it. It was requested that this man be given an extension of time for a period of one year. That is commonly done-but in this instance it was refused. I found out afterwards that in that very year, when they refused to extend his time for one year, they had retained over four hundred employees in similar circumstances. The company did not in fact save anything by their action in regard to this man. The truth is that they lost money because they had to pay him his pension as well as pay the man who replaced him. I repeat that in the

The Address-Mr. Manion
year when they refused to extend his time they extended the terms of over four hundred other employees. Yet I was refused. So far as I remember those are the only occasions in my term as Minister of Railways and Canals that I in any way attempted to interfere.
I will admit this, that I did interfere with headquarters. I endeavoured to bring down and did bring down the salaries of men at headquarters. To my mind most extravagant salaries were being paid, salaries which were not necessary at all. I will admit, too, that I succeeded in bringing down those salaries. I have stated on other occasions, and I state again to-night, that in salaries at headquarters alone we cut off over $1,000,000 in expenses. In other words, we decreased salaries by over
SI.000.000, and I believe we improved the efficiency of the road by so doing.
So far as wages are concerned, may I point out that I had nothing to do with them, neither has the present Minister of Transport. I never did interfere with wages, and I am sure he has not interfered with them. Neither of us would have had the power to do so.
Then the depression came on in 1929. It began a year before my hon. friends opposite left office, and it continued until 1933. On account of the huge losses which both railways *were facing, it was found necessary to try to impress upon the management that they must cut down expenditures. It was to this cutting of expenses that I referred a few moments ago. Possibly I would do well to give one or two illustrations. One man in particular-and I can give his name, because he is not now in the country-a Mr. Gaston, was drawing $62,000 a year. Why he was being paid that amount I could not find out. The people who complained to me about Gaston were the president and officers of the Canadian National Railways. They told me he was getting $62,000 a year and doing nothing for it, and he was lording it over them all, to use an expression of the street. He was dismissed and sent back to the United States, from where he had come.
Another man named Hummel was getting $35,000 a year, and he was sent back. Without any reflection upon my friends opposite I say that on the railway at that time there were a number of officers from the United States who were not necessary, and who were drawing large salaries, and we sent a number of them back to the United States where they belonged.
This was the only interference we made with the management of the Canadian National. We did that through the board of directors, as we had a perfect right to do. There is
nothing wrong with the present minister protesting to the board, if he thinks they are too extravagant, and asking them to cut down expenses. If they are extravagant, in his opinion, he is not doing his duty if he does not protest. I did protest and brought about a great many of these changes.
I want to make it quite clear that in speaking of Americans I have not and never did have any antagonism to them, but at the same time I do believe that our Canadian National, and the Canadian Pacific for that matter, can be run just as well by Canadians as by anybody from any other country in the world.
Another charge was that I closed the railway shops in various sections of this country. I do not think it was the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) who made that charge, but some other hon. member did. Some of the shops of both the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific were closed; but far from closing them, I actually arranged with the government of which I was a member, to lend the two railways money, hundreds of thousands of dollars, to keep the shops going. In fact we were criticized for lending money to the Canadian Pacific. My hon. friends opposite have done a certain amount of that since they have come into office, but we did it when conditions were bad; when the shop men were in a terrible plight. We did lend money to the two railways to help them keep their shops going, and the money was paid back in full by the Canadian Pacific.
What they were referring to in London, I believe, was that we had given contracts for building freight cars and engines outside the railway shops. But that has always been done. Only within recent months contracts amounting to some millions of dollars have been given by the present management for building cars, and perhaps engines, by private companies. I am speaking subject to correction; but I read the item in the press, and I take it for granted that it is true. I offer no criticism because that is the proper thing to do. We have in this country a number of big car manufacturing companies. Have they not some rights? I know that this action was protested by some men working for the Canadian National and by some men on the Canadian Pacific who contended that the railways should build these cars in their own shops. We did give the railway shops some of that sort of work to do; but they did not have the equipment, and it would have taken millions of dollars to install the equipment. On the other hand, there were companies like the Canada Car, the National Steel Car of
The Address-Mr. Manion

Hamilton, the Eastern Car, the Canadian Locomotive Company of Kingston, and other large Canadian companies, and it would have been most unfair to these companies-

speechtext: Why?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Because, after all, the
people who have put their money into Canada Car, National Steel Car and these other big Canadian companies I have mentioned, are Canadians too, and, in addition, their employees have rights. Surely we do not owe everything to the employees of the two railways. There are other Canadians just as good as the railway men.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How about the rights of all the people of Canada who, as we all know, have invested their money in the Canadian National?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
On the contrary, most of
the money invested in the Canadian National came from the United States, and eighty-five per cent of the money invested in the Canadian Pacific is money from England. I am not belittling the bondholders at all. But I say that we took hundreds of thousands of dollars out of the treasury to keep the railway shops open and to pay the deficit on the Canadian National. I have forgotten the exact amount, but hon. gentlemen opposite will have to supply the deficit for last year amounting to approximately one million dollars a week. So I repeat, without any offence to the men on the Canadian National and the men on the Canadian Pacific, that these other large Canadian companies have been established for the purpose of manufacturing railway cars, and they and their employees have rights too.
By the way, I should like to interject that the management of both railways were insistent that these contracts should be given to these companies because they contended that these companies had been built up for that purpose, and that if we destroyed them- and Canadian Car had been closed for four or five years-there were no other private companies in Canada to do this work. These private companies had a great many employees who had been out of work a long time, longer than most of the men on the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, and they naturally had to be taken care of.
Another charge related to amalgamation. The hon. gentleman accused me directly of starting the amalgamation of the two roads when I brought in the two bills for the consolidation of the telegraph and express business of the two railways. Before dealing with that, I should like to show the attitude of this party towards amalgamation.
TMr. Manion.]
Let me recall to hon. gentlemen that in the first place we brought in a bill in 1933, which was passed, the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, the last clause of which, clause 27 of part IV, reads as follows:
Nothing in this act shall he deemed to authorize the amalgamation of any railway company which is comprised in National railways, with any railway company which is comprised in Pacific railways-
That means the Canadian Pacific Railway.

nor to authorize the unified management and control of the railway system which forms part of National railways with the^ railway system which forms part of Pacific railways.
That is perfectly clear, and that was put in by us in the act of 1933. But that is not all. The speech of the former leader of this party has been many times quoted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
May I
ask my hon. friend, was not that clause put in as an amendment from the opposition of that day?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not think so.

speechtext: It was put in at the instance of the opposition.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am not going to quarrel
with that statement because I do not recall the exact circumstances. At all events the government of the day took responsibility for the legislation, and at that time we had almost as big a majority as hon. gentlemen opposite have.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Not quite as large, but
we had 140 members and the government now has only about 170.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Wait until the next time,
when we will change that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We have 180.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is far too many. At any rate we were in power at the time this clause was put into the bill. I am not going to dispute with my hon. friends who say that it was their clause. If the government had not agreed to it, it would not have been put in. I want to be quite fair. I shall be glad to have the records searched because frankly I do not recall it as hon. gentlemen opposite give it. At any rate that clause is in the bill, and we put it in there; there is no doubt about that.
Then my former leader, Mr. Bennett, made a speech in Winnipeg laying down the policy from which we never departed. Everybody

The Address-Mr. Manion
remembers the phrase: "Amalgamation never; competition ever." We never at any time departed from that.
Finally there was the resolution passed at the national convention of the Conservative party last July. I thought I had it here, but I cannot lay my hand on it at the moment. At all events the convention passed a resolution absolutely opposing anything in the way of amalgamation or unification of the two railways. Eveiybody knows that. I am not going to argue it. We are on record over and over again as opposed to amalgamation or unification or anything of that sort. I do not think I should have to be arguing the question at all. I have been opposing unification since 1934.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question while we are on a discussion of the subject of what happened to the railways? During the period that my hon. friend was Minister of Railways, why were twice as many Canadian National trains cut off from Saskatchewan as compared with Canadian Pacific trains?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, I did not have anything to do with the cutting off of trains, but I assume that it was for the reason that the Canadian National Railways thought there had been too many trains and that perhaps they had better cut some of them off. I had nothing to do at any time with cutting off any trains at any place. That was the function of the management. If they cut them off, my hon. friend had better protest to the management. It is the same management now as it was when we went out of power.
I have just said that I have opposed unification since 1934. Incidentally, although I do not want to get into a political controversy, I have not noticed any ministers of this government opposing it. I believe that my right hon. friend is opposed to unification, but I should like to hear him say so sometimes.

speechtext: I am afraid the right hon. gentleman is speaking below his breath. He has not been saying it at any place I know of, and I challenge him to do so now.

speechtext: I say it now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am glad I have been able to stir up the right hon. gentleman to something, because I am afraid that he has not been saying it, nor has any member of his government that I can recall, in several years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, I think they had better begin to question it. As a matter of fact, the only man in this house who ever came out for amalgamation was the Minister of Trade and Commerce. (Mr. Euler).
