But always under public
ownership.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: All right. But I do not know that the men who would be put out of work by the amalgamation of the two roads would care much whether they were put out through government or through private ownership. I say that my hon. friend is the only member that I know of who has ever come out flatly for amalgamation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite
wrong. There used to be an independent Conservative member from Toronto who was strongly in favour of it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Who was he?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. W. F. Maclean.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, well, Maclean is dead long ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Perhaps it might be unfair to say that there are some other members of his party who are dead but who don't know it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I don't know whether the hon. gentleman refers to me, but if he thinks that I am dead and don't know it I hope I shall let him know the contrary before this session is over. Billy Maclean, however, has been dead for ten or fifteen years, and if we have to hunt in the grave for a Conservative who supported amalgamation I think it reinforces my argument. I was afraid my hon. friend might contradict my statement, so I brought his speech here, but I do not need to read it. At any rate, out of the two hundred and forty-five members of this house only one has come out for amalgamation or unification. This house is a pretty good cross-section of the country, and I think it is well worth the while of those who believe in unification to remember that fact. I did not intend, however, to go into that, especially.
I wish now to deal with the bills which I tried to introduce into the house in 1934. I tried, but I was stopped. I did, however, bring them before the committee. I am going to deal with this incident as honestly as I have dealt with all these questions. In 1934 the express bill and the telegraph bill were brought to my attention by Sir Edward Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and by Judge Fullerton, then chairman of the Canadian National Railways. Both these gentlemen wrote me exactly the same letter
The Address-Mr. Manion

asking me to introduce those two bills into the house. I protested that they should do it themselves.
I will give the evidence of that fact, but first I shall give a brief survey of the circumstances. They claimed that it was too late for them to introduce those measures as private bills. They said that to do so would cost them $11,000, and they asked us as a government to bring them in. I took them before the select standing committee on railways and shipping on June 20, 1934, without having introduced them into this house. That was a rather informal proceeding, but it was done because the committee was sitting and I thought it should know what suggestion had been made by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. Sir Edward Beatty was not present, but Mr. Fullerton attended for the Canadian National Railways; Mr. Apps, representing Sir Edward Beatty, appeared for the Canadian Pacific Railway; Mr. Hungerford was also present for the Canadian National Railways, and they supported those bills.
May I interrupt for a moment my line of argument to say that I did not think, when the two railways asked me to introduce these two bills, I could have refused. I have thought a great deal over the matter, and I do not believe I am wrong in suggesting that if the heads of the two railways were to come to the Minister of Transport and ask him to bring forward some bill which-as in the case of those bills-was not in conflict with anything the government had supported, he could refuse to do so. I think he would be in exactly the same position as I was in at that time. A minister of railways is the minister of all the railways in Canada. In this house he is the mouthpiece of the Canadian National Railways, but he deals as far as the government is concerned with the other railways of the country as well, and practically the only other railway is the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I am going to read part of the evidence, the only part which bears on the matter, from the minutes of the meeting of the standing committee on railways and shipping on June 20, 1934, which is towards the end of the session. I shall quote myself. I said to the committee:
Gentlemen-The two railways wrote me some time ago and in a moment I will read the letter, and when I do so if you will transpose the words "express company" for "telegraph company" that will cover the letter in both cases. The Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National have got together and they want to unite into subsidiary companies their express companies and their telegraph companies-communications as they call them-as two separate companies. I will read one of the letters they have written to me, and the other is exactly

the same except that it deals with the other question. This letter is signed by Mr. Fullerton and Mr. Beatty for their prospective companies the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, and it is addressed to me:-
"We are enclosing herewith draft of bill incorporating the Canadian Railway Express Company which our companies desire to have passed at the present session of parliament as a means of implementing the recommendation of the royal commission on transportation respecting the conduct of express business of the two companies.
"You will observe that the proposed legislation is simply the incorporation of the new company with the requisite powers to carry on the express business of the two companies if, as and when the trustees of the Canadian National and the directors of the Canadian Pacific determine that this should be done.
"We regard it as essential that the legislation should be passed at the earliest possible moment in order to expedite whatever measures of economy and efficiency our two companies may jointly decide should be adopted."
This is signed by Mr. Fullerton and Mr. Beatty. The same letter refers also to the communications company except it is communications instead of express.
I shall read another paragraph. It is myself speaking again.
They should have brought them in as a private bill, which I prefer they should do. However, they pointed out in the first place there were some heavy fees which, of course, parliament could have waived, amounting to something like $11,000. In addition to that there were the delays that could not have been got over this session. I am willing to bring these in as government measures, but since this committee was sitting I thought I should lay these bills before this committee and have a gesture of approval in a general way. The bills are here; I have four copies; they have not been introduced-
To parliament, I meant.
-but I have them ready to introduce this afternoon if the committee agrees. I might read one of the bills for you-they differ only in so far as one deals with "express" and the other with "communications"; otherwise they are practically the same.
I do not need to read any more. That is the introduction, the informal introduction of the matter to the railway committee, on which were sitting the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power), and, I believe, the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray); probably he was not there that day, because his name does not appear on the record, as it usually did when he was present. These hon. members and others were on that committee. I repeat that I dealt informally with those bills before the committee in order to get the opinion of the committee. The only protests made against the bills came from one Conservative, Doctor Price, and one Liberal, Mr. Hanbury, former member for

The Address-Mr. Manion
Vancouver-Burrard. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) and the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) took part in the discussion. The former asked a question with respect to the allotment of stock. He wanted to be sure that the Canadian National would be on the same basis as the Canadian Pacific, and rightly so. The Minister of Pensions and National Health took no attitude against the bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He took the hon. member's advice. It is always so good.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member's defence is always good, too. That, however, is a little aside. As hon. gentlemen know, there was a dinner to-night to the returned soldier members of the house, and the Minister of Pensions and National Health defended me in a mock case in which I was charged.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member had better hire me again.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He defended me so well that I was acquitted. As I say, Mr. Speaker, no one opposed the bills except Doctor Price of Moncton, and Mr. Hanbury of Vancouver. And they did not oppose them on the ground that there was any danger of amalgamation of the railways. Doctor Price took the view, in which he was supported by Mr. Hanbury, that the effect of such legislation would be to cut down the telegraph service in the mari-times. Apart from that, however, he offered no opposition. Mr. Hungerford took part in the discussion. Perhaps I might quote my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have before me certain passages which I have marked. I am not trying to misrepresent him or anyone else, and naturally not myself. Let me quote:
Hon. Mr. Euler: Before I say anything about the control of that company, I would like to ask whether that, in any sense, comes in any conflict with the clauses of the bill we put through last year?
He is referring to the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific bill.
Hon. Mr. Manion: No, that was about amalgamation. I will read that clause. I have it marked. It says in clause 27, part 4....
Then I read the clause which I have quoted to the house. I continued:
I read that clause which enabled it; it is under part 2, clause 16 in regard to cooperation.
And then I quoted the clause:
-without restricting the generality of the foregoing, any such measures, plans or arrangements may include and be effected by means of-
(a) new companies controlled by stock ownership, equitably apportioned between the companies.
Let me next quote what Mr. Hanbury said:
Mr. Hanbury:	I would be interested in
knowing whether the railway commission has any control over the rates of the telegraph and express companies and the services that they shall render. Perhaps Judge Fullerton can give us some information on that.
Hon. Mr. Fullerton:	They have over the
rates, certainly.
Mr. Hanbury:	Not over the services?
Hon. Mr. Fullerton:	I am not sure about
that.
Mr. Hanbury:	I find myself to a considerable
extent in agreement with Dr. Price, but perhaps I am on a little different basis from him in that regard. I did not favour the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National bill last year; I opposed it. . . . True, I recognize the bill passed last year did contemplate such amalgamation as is now suggested; whereas the bill contemplated and forbade any amalgamation of the railway services. If I accepted these bills, it would simply be on this basis, that the legislation is now in effect, and it is perhaps not our duty to put any impediments in the way of the railway companies carrying out the wishes of parliament as expressed in the bill. But my personal view of this matter is, I am opposed to it; I do not think it is true economy, and I think that the people of Canada would suffer from the lack of competitive services in the future.
Hon. Mr. Euler:	Mr. Chairman, I have
always in the past, as I think many of the committee know, been in favour of doing everything possible to effect economies on the Canadian National Railways; and to that extent, I am entirely in favour of any legislation that may carry out that intention. The only thing that occurs to me in connection with the bill is this: in the new company, the only shareholders will be the C.P.R. and the C.N.R., I take it. Is that correct? They are the only ones that may be shareholders?
Hon. Mr. Manion:	Of course, they may issue
capital or preference stock, so I suppose they may sell it.
Hon. Mr. Euler:	I think the committee
should know whether it is the intention that this new company shall consist only of the C.P.R. and the C.N.R., or whether the outside public will be invited to subscribe.
Without going further, I repeat that the hon. gentleman took the attitude, which I think was a right one, that the Canadian Pacific Railway should not have any greater share than the Canadian National. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) was also on the committee, and I shall quote what he said:
Mr. Bothwell:	I should like to ask a question in regard to those two departments, the telegraphs and express departments. Have those two departments been losing the Canadian National and the C.P.R., or have they been paying their way? I think the committee would like to get information in connection with that.
Mr. Fairweather:	That is a very difficult
question to answer.
The facts are as I have stated. The only objection came from one Liberal, Mr. Han-
The Address-Mr. Manion

bury, and one Conservative, Doctor Price. Neither the Minister of Pensions and National Health, nor the Minister of Trade and Commerce, nor anybody else objected to those bills except from the point of view of their working out in detail. No one in the committee expressed any opinion which suggested that there was anything wrong with those bills.
The next step in the process was to bring them into the house. As I say, the committee raised no objection. Doctor Price and Mr. Hanbury took exception to them only on the ground that they would result in a diminished service. That was June 20. On June 21 I attempted to introduce them into the House of Commons. May I quote what I said on that occasion:
The bill, for leave to introduce which I am now asking, commits no one to anything; it is simply an enabling bill, the purpose of which is to permit the companies, if finally they come to an agreement, to carry out this measure. They have not yet come to such agreement and there is no certainty that they will; but both railways, through Mr. Beatty and Mr. Fullerton respectively, have written to me asking me to introduce these two bills and to endeavour to have them adopted by the house. . . .
The government had no information in regard to the matter, because the railway companies did not request us until very recently to introduce these bills. Apparently they had not arrived at the position of discussing an agreement of this kind until quite recently, when they wrote to me, and naturally I preferred that they should submit the bills themselves. They could have done so except for want of time, and they have asked us to deal with the matter	
Mr. Gray: Is this bill a first step towards the amalgamation of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway?
Mr. Manion: This is not a step towards the amalgamation of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. I shall explain the matter when it is before the house, but I may say that what is contemplated here is permitted under the act of last year with respect to subsidiary companies.
The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) I believe, was the only one who objected to the bills being introduced without notice, and, of course, it was his right to do so. Then on June 25, four days later, I withdrew the bills. I shall read everything that appears in Hansard with respect to them. That was the day I withdrew them. I quote:
On the order for the introduction of bills to incorporate Canadian Railway Express Company and Canadian Communications Company:
Hon. R. J. Manion (Minister of Railways): Regarding these two bills, the government was asked by the two railway companies to introduce them, as they regarded it as essential that enabling: legislation should be made avail-

able to expedite whatever measures for unified operation the two companies might decide jointly to adopt with respect to the two subsidiary services referred to. However, latest information intimates that no agreement has as yet been reached or is in prospect of being reached at an early date, if at all. Therefore the matter cannot be said to be one of immediate urgency. For this reason the government does not intend to proceed with these bills.
I withdrew the bills. That is the whole record of them. Though I have not read all the discussion before the railway committee, I have given the gist of it and I have read practically everything pertinent that appears in Hansard indicating why we withdrew them. They were withdrawn because they were not justified. I discovered, after the letters had been written to me, that no agreement had been reached. For that reason we did not introduce them. They had nothing to do with the amalgamation of the railways. I have shown that we were opposed to amalgamation, and evidence to that effect appeared in our legislation. We were against amalgamation, and I trust there will be no more misquotations.
So far as cooperation is concerned, it was recommended by the Duff commission which examined fully the whole railway problem of Canada, and it was inserted in the bill in 1933, which bill was intended in part to give the railways an opportunity to cooperate.
Finally the railway labour unions of Canada put on record last year before the senate committee their request for cooperation. I have their statement right here and it may be well to read it. One of the labour leaders showed me the statements himself and indicated that they were favourable to cooperation. This is the statement:
Memorandum of comments and recommendations.
Submitted by the dominion joint legislative committee of the Railway Transportation Brotherhoods and the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, to the special committee of the senate appointed to inquire into and report upon the best means of relieving the country from its extremely serious railway situation and financial burden consequent thereto.
I shall give just two quotations which cover their recommendations about cooperation.
In the review and comments here submitted, we have endeavoured to bring to your attention the effects upon the Canadian people as a whole which, in our opinion, would occur from amalgamation, unification, abandonment or further pooling of services. If, in the judgment of those in authority, there must be further cooperative measures, effect to such action should not be taken unless and until provision is made whereby labour's interests are protected and compensated for loss. In the consideration of any such measures, railway

The Address-Mr. Manion
labour will be found ready and willing to sit clown with others concerned and give sympathetic consideration to all practical and humane proposals submitted.
On another page they say as follows:
It is respectfully submitted on behalf of railway labour that if the interest on capital expenditures for unused power and rolling stock of the railways, or of unused plant or equipment in industry, due to depression or falling off of business, constitutes legitimate overhead charges against the consumer, it seems to logically follow that unem 'loyed W'orkers from similar causes should have an equally legitimate claim upon a larger share from industry as compensation for the loss of employment opportunity. Moreover, in any further cooperative measures involving labour displacement, definite provision should be made for equitable treatment to railway labour by compensation from the industry for any and all loss of employment opportunity.
With that I fully agree. I know no reason why, if those who propose unification take the attitude that men displaced must be cared for, those who suggest cooperation should not take the same attitude. There are opportunities for cooperation; we see them all around us: two ticket offices down here on Sparks street within a couple of hundred feet of each other, and a similar situation in practically all the big cities of Canada. There is the Montreal terminal, the hotels in Vancouver- the recent agreement by the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific in regard to using one hotel instead of two is one of the best illustrations of what cooperation could do. AH those measures could be carried out without hurting anyone, particularly if the men were cared for as proposed by the labour men, with which proposal I entirely agree. So far as enforced cooperation is concerned, there were those of us who thought that since the railways did not show much sign of voluntary cooperation, enforced cooperation might be worth considering. But in view of the attitude taken by Sir Edward Beatty, speaking for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company before the senate committee, enforced cooperation appears to be out of the question.
Two other points I want to raise. One is the " crucifixion " so-called of Sir Henry Thornton. The statement has been made many times; it was made in the London by-election and made all across this country; on one occasion I remember I was charged with killing Sir Henry Thornton.. The fact is that Sir Henry Thornton resigned and a year later he died of cancer. I did not have much to do with that. And never in the years I knew Sir Henry Thornton did I have a cross word of any kind with him. We were good friends throughout, despite the fact that I accepted his resignation. I say to-night
what I have said in many places-and I think I have written it once or twice-that he was a very able man; that he brought about in . the Canadian National Railways an esprit de corps which was of great value, and did good work in many ways. But I have pointed out-and it was no discredit to him-that he had this fault, that he did not know the value of money. I doubt whether anyone in this house who knew him well would think of contradicting that statement in view of the decreases in cost of operation amounting to $19,000,000, in view of the extravagance in such things as hotels, the Montreal terminal proposals to cost some $50,000,000, the building of those ships on the Pacific. In view of that, I do not think anyone would say that I am unjust in saying that extravagance was his great fault.
There was one other matter that was not his fault, namely, that there was not proper control over Sir Henry Thornton. He was a dominating personality and took complete control of the board of directors instead of their controlling him. As a result there was wild extravagance in the Canadian National Railways under his regime. One of the hon. members for Halifax referred to the fact that there were a great many defunct railroads unloaded on the Canadian National which are unprofitable and on which the Canadian National has to bear the capital charges. Practically every down-at-heel railway in this country was taken over by the Canadian National; most of them never paid their way. But there were other things-and in this I am a little critical-

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that Sir Henry Thornton was responsible for taking over those defunct railways?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He was, at any rate, partly responsible, because he was the head of the Canadian National. If I must give an answer to my hon. friend-I do not like to, because it will not please him-the people really responsible were the government which he supports.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend does not mean to imply that there were anywhere near the number of so-called defunct railways taken over during Sir Henry Thornton's management as were taken over when the Canadian National system was originally put together. And certainly this government was never responsible for that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, quite right; in 1919 when all the railways were taken over, I suppose those railways were greater in length than the defunct railways taken over when
The Address-Mr. Manion

the hon. member-was Minister of Railways. I was not going to mention my hon. friend, but he was Minister of Railways when all these extravagant outlays were made by the Canadian National, and he was the man who should have held Sir Henry back from the wild extravagance that went on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be glad to defend at any time anything I ever put before this house. And my hon. friend never opposed any of them.

Well, perhaps that is true. My hon. friends were the government, and conditions in the country were pretty good. But they took over all the defunct railways, as we well remember, nearly all that were left when the Canadian National was organized. Take, for example, the Quebec Southern. I looked over the file, and I must say it was disgraceful; that railway was taken over when my hon. friend was Minister of Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

I do not blame him for taking them over, but I blame the parties who pressed the government to do it and the government which permitted them to press it into taking over this lot of defunct roads which became a charge on the Canadian National. Probably Sir Henry Thornton should have put his foot down and said, No; but while the railway administration, like these other boards and commissions, was theoretically independent, they were subject to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the interest of accuracy I must say again that my hon. friend's expression " defunct railways " is entirely incorrect. The number of railways taken over during the time I was Minister of Railways in the former government of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was in fact very small indeed compared with those which had been taken over by the preceding administration.

Oh, I do not compare the railways that I described as defunct, with the whole Canadian National. I do not agree to-day that the old Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk should have been taken over by this country. I do not want to go into that question now, but I say they should have been allowed to go into bankruptcy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So do I. I said so at the time.

I agree with the hon. gentleman. I was a member of the house then;

but I was a young member, had been a member for a year, I did not presume to put my opinion up against that of senior men, or the government of that time; but, looking back, I think they should have been allowed to go into bankruptcy. But my hon. friend was Minister of Railways in 1929. In 1929, a pre-election year, between $200,000,000 and $250,000,000 was added to the debt of the Canadian National Railways in all kinds of political expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no.

Oh, yes. I have put them on record, and my speeches will show them. I could give the record very easily. I did not want to get into this, but my hon. friend would interrupt me though I was not mentioning him at all. He was Minister of Railways at the time. I repeat, in that one year, the year before the election of 1930, they added to the debt of the Canadian National Railways by upwards of $200,000,000. I used the figure of $250,000,000 on another occasion here, but perhaps I was in error by a few million, so I shall cut it down to between $200,000,000 and $250,000,000. Not only that; but between 1921 and 1930, when the party of my hon. friend was in power continuously except for a few months in 1926, they added $32,000,000 to the annual interest charges of the Canadian National Railways. During a number of those years the hon. gentleman was Minister of Railways. In that time $20,000,000 was added to the interest owing to the bondholders and $12,000,000 to the interest on money owing to the government.
Would my hon. friend be good enough to tell us how much was added to the annual income of the railway during those years?

There was a good deal added to the income of the railway during those years, yes; but so far as I remember- I am speaking from memory but I think I am correct-in only two years in all the time the Canadian National Railways have existed have they paid their interest charges; so my hon. friend was not doing so well. But at any rate my hon. friend who asked me the question would not deny that in the nine years between 1921 and 1930 there was $20,000,000 added to the annual interest payable to bondholders and $12,000,000 to the annual interest on money owing to the government, so that was a pretty good piece of work. Take, for example, the Montreal terminal. Does anybody suggest to-day that a $50,000,000 expenditure on a Montreal terminal, such as was

The Address-Mr. Manion
started in 1929 and on which $17,000,000, I think, was spent before we came into office, was justified?

Of course.
Mr. FOURNIER (Maisonneuve-Rosemount) We deserve it.

You may deserve it for unemployment relief, but I do not admit that $50,000,000 was ever justified at any time for one station for the Canadian National Railways in the city of Montreal. I do not notice any of the ministers saying they think it is justified, as my hon. friend does; but probably he is thinking of the votes that would be forthcoming as a result of the work on the terminal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For a station, did my hon. friend say?
For a terminal, mostly a station.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no.
Yes, yes. I know just as much as my hon. friend does about this railway. I shall not take a back seat to my hon. friend or anybody else in this house on this railway question. I know it pretty well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want my hon. friend to take a back seat, but some of us know a little about it.
I am not questioning that.
Did my hon. friend vote against that $50,000,000 when it went through this house?

I have repeated in this
house that during those years the Canadian National was so strong under Sir Henry Thornton that I do not suppose I did; I do not suppose anybody did. Conditions in Canada were pretty fair, and we were not questioning these expenditures. But the fact that I did not happen to vote against it, does not lessen the mistake. I have made mistakes in my time, and I cannot say positively but that I might have done the same if I had been minister; I do not know. I do say, however, that the fact that I may have made a mistake or that I did not vote against it does not justify my hon. friends in adding from $200,000,000 to $250,000,000 to the debt of the railway in one year, and certainly it does not justify the construction of a $50,000,000 terminal in Montreal. If that were justified, I would ask my hon. friends this: We have been out of power since 1935. We stopped work on that terminal in either 1930 or 1931; I do not remember the exact time, but it was probably 1931 when 71492-37J
we halted further expenditures on it. About; $17,000,000 was the amount that had been spent on that work prior to that time, which would leave $33,000,000 to be spent to complete it, Hon. gentlemen opposite have been in power for nearly four years, and why is it that they have not completed the terminal? If it is justified, why did they not complete it? They knew it was never justified. That is why they did not continue the work and complete it, and that is the whole reason. By the way, ire. reference to the hon. gentleman who has been asking me questions, may I say that there was no greater extravagance ever committed, in proportion to size, than the construction of the hotel in Saskatoon at a cost of $4,000,000. The hon. gentleman comes from Saskatoon,
It did not cost $4,000,000.

Well, it did. The hon.
gentleman had better look up his figures.
I know them pretty well.
It was pretty close to
It was a long distance from $4,000,000.

Then perhaps that was
because we cut it down.

That was what was wrong
with the Canadian National all the time; you were cutting them down.
Order.

I do not mind the hon.
gentleman getting a little excited. He is fighting for Saskatoon, and I do not blame him.
Fighting for what is right.

That is debatable. There
was nothing right in building a $4,000,000 hotel in Saskatoon when the best they could possibly have supported there, according to what I am told by the best hotelkeepers in this' country, was a $1,000,000 hotel. Perhaps $4,000,000 may be the wrong amount, but I am using round figures.

My hon. friend does not
think very much of the city of Saskatoon.

I think a great deal of
Saskatoon, but my hon. friend is just trying to play a little cheap politics now. I am just as honest about the city of Saskatoon as I am about the city of Montreal; that is all. I want to ask, Mr. Speaker, if that $50,000,000 expenditure in Montreal was justified in 1929, why has that work not been completed sinee 1935? It must be because the government

And the best of it is that
he carries out his promises.

My hon. friend says the Minister of Public Works carries out his promises; but this has nothing to do with public works; he is making a promise for the Minister of Transport, a promise that the Minister of Transport, if anybody, had a right to make. I continue quoting:
At an afternoon meeting in Atwater Market Hon. Fernand Rinfret, Secretary of State, had made a similar pledge to the two thousand electors who attended. Both statements clarified and amplified the declaration of Mr. Rinfret on Friday that the Liberal government would "fill the hole on Dorchester street."

That was on January 17. Two days previously the Secretary of State is quoted, according to the same newspaper, the Gazette, as follows:
Mr. Rinfret said the tunnel under the Lachine bridge to connect St. Paul with St. Henry ward would be brought to fruition shortly.
May I ask the hon. member for St. Henry if the tunnel has been built?
No.

I thought they always
kept their promises. My hon. friend said that the Liberals always kept their promises. They still have a few months to go before the next election, so they may start the work after all.
He also stated the abandoned Canadian National railway works project conceived prior to 1930, and which involved disappearance of the level crossings in St. 11 rnry. would also be resumed, and this would mean an end of the "hole" on Dorchester street. ... "I declare that while the federal government is anxious to restore conditions by providing as much employment as possible, there is no intention to allow one man to starve in Canada."
I do not think there should be any starvation under a Liberal regime.
"So long as there are unemployed there will be direct relief for men, their wives and children. We will do our part, and if the municipal powers, and provincial powers should become fatigued, be tranquil. While there is a single unemployed, the federal government will see to their sustenance. It is not an independent who will do that. It is not a man-"
This is Mr. Houde-
"-isolated from all parties who can do anything. He may make eloquent speeches, even enact farces, but I am autliorized to repeat to you that as long as there are unemployed in Montreal, even if we are alone, the federal government engages itself on honour to give sustenance to him, his wife and children."
And yet the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), when I asked him the other day about conditions in Nova Scotia, and called his attention to a telegram I had received,-no wonder he looks down at his book-told me that that was the duty, as I should know, of the province and the municipality. He had better fight it out with the Secretary of State over there.
Then, this was stated-and I believe it is by the present Secretary of State, one of the two gentlemen over there-and they won the election, too.

Hear, hear.

The Address-Mr. Manion

But we won in Waterloo
South. The election in question was against Mr. Houde. This is the statement I find:
Pledges action on C.N.R. The government of which I am a part will settle this problem of the Canadian National Railways, and the level crossings. We will fill the hole on Dorchester street, and solve the problem of the approaches thereto.
Mr.	DUPUIS:	Is	the	hon.	gentleman
against the terminal in Montreal?

I am certainly against $50,000,000 being spent on the terminal, just the same as the hon. member's own party is against it. Otherwise something would have been done in the last four years. The party opposite has been in power for four years.
Mr.	DUPUIS:	Is	the	hon.	gentleman
satisfied with the station in Montreal?

No, I am not satisfied. I do not think that hole in the ground should be left. But certainly I do not like to overtax the dominion on account of the Canadian National Railways, for political purposes. I say here solemnly to-night to those who are the friends of the Canadian National Railways, and particularly to the employees of that railway system, that the surest way to destroy the system is to play politics of that kind with it.
Then we have this humorous side of the matter. To show how far-sighted my hon. friends opposite are, politically, Mr. Hunger-ford has said, on their behalf, that $12,500,000 will be spent over a period of three or four years. Not only do they provide at this time for the coming election, but they are providing for the next one, too. I must confess that some day I am going to ask them to start a summer school at Port Hope for Conservative politicians. We know nothing about playing politics, when it gets down to that sort of business.
But I must say seriously that there is no surer way of destroying the Canadian National Railways than by playing politics of that kind with it. There is a campaign going on across the country, one which is gaining ground among business men, without doubt, for something by way of unification of these two railways. And with the increased deficit of the Canadian National Railways, $10,000,000 more than last' year, as it is reported, and with these increased expenditures for political purposes in connection with the filling of this hole in the city of Montreal there is the great danger that the Canadian National Railways will be destroyed by those who claim they are its friends.
I would not have taken so long, Mr. Speaker, but hon. members opposite have had some responsibility for the length of my speech.
I have, however, almost finished, and I shall leave plenty of time to take the vote tonight. I wish to repeat that the depression came upon us in 1929. The Conservative party was elected in 1930, and we were forced to bring about economies. We did that for the Canadian National Railways and, to their credit, my hon. friends opposite to a large extent have carried on in the same manner. I think, generally speaking, they have played a pretty fair game in the country. I do not think they have been doing much in the way of politics-until now, in connection with that hole in the ground in the city of Montreal.
I come back to the matter at this time because my observations were interrupted iby the Minister of Finance. I was discussing the suggestion that Sir Henry Thornton was supposed to have been crucified by me. I said to the directors that they must bring about economy. We were being asked to put up too much money at a time when relief was costing so much. I pleaded here, with the railway committee which was sitting in the house, to cut the extravagant expenditures. But Sir Henry Thornton declared, in a manner which he had of opposing economies, against these economies. I could repeat what I said earlier-and it is the only word I would say against him-he seemed to lack sufficient knowledge of the value of money, whether his own or anybody else's.
Would the hon. member permit a question? What is the value of money, may I ask?
I can quite understand my social credit friend asking what is the value of money, because if there is anybody on God's green earth that does not know the value of it, it is the social credit party.
I was simply looking for enlightenment. That was a cheap, political answer.

The hon. member says he was looking for light. I can understand why any social crediter would be looking for light. If there is any group which sees darkness more completely around it than the social crediters, I do not know who they are. But if the hon. member-
But the hon. member has not answered the question yet.

Well, I suggest that the hon. member go and ask Mr. Aberhart.

The Address-Mr. Manion
I believe I could get an answer from him.

The hon. member says he believes he can get an answer. I place his answer on Hansard, because I think it should be there. The people of Alberta have been looking for that answer now, at $25 a month, for a long time.
I would ask the hon. member how that $25 a month for the people of Alberta is going to be paid, after the mess this government, and the party of which the hon. member is leader, made of the railways?

During the rest of the session I am going to try to show the mess that the leader of the present government has made of things. Surely the hon. member did ;not expect me to stop my discussion of the railways to explain what money means? iEvery other hon. member in the house but the hon. gentleman in question knew what I meant when I said that Sir Henry Thornton did not know the value of money.
Leave Sir Henry alone- a dead man.

I am not saying anything against anybody. But I do not need any instructions from the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, about ethics or anything else. I just make that suggestion to him, and I do not think I need any instructions from him at all as to how I should treat either the dead or the living. I am not saying anything offensive about Sir Henry at all. I am pointing out the opinion of everybody else in Canada, from the right hon. gentleman before me right down to the ordinary employee in the Canadian National railways.
Now, I had better finish, because we want to vote to-night.

Before the hon. member finishes, I should like to ask a question. An article from the Gazette which I have in my hand has refreshed my memory. I wonder if he is the same Doctor Manion who is quoted in the Montreal Gazette of November, 1927, as having said in Toronto:
I believe the Conservative party has been too honest in the past. Our party in the past has been too honest in strictly defining its position and policy on controversial and sectional questions.

Yes, I am the man who
said that, and I believe it yet. I shall explain that statement, since the hon. member has raised it, although it has nothing to do with the railways. I should like, however, to give an answer to my good friend over there. I said a few moments ago I wished the Liberal
JMr. Manion.]
party would establish a summer school for Conservatives at Port Hope and let us go there to learn politics, because they play them so well. In that remark I wras referring to the stupid habit, to my mind, of some Conservatives of occasionally grabbing controversial questions and jumping into them without any reason at all for discussing them at that particular time. I do not see the reason for my hon. friends opposite-they are a little wiser than we are in that respect- or for ourselves jumping into all kinds of controversial questions and insisting on fighting them to a finish when there is no occasion for a fight at all. It is just shadow-boxing. That is what I was referring to, and I am not ashamed of it at all.
I hope I shall not be interrupted any more, Mr. Speaker, because I wish to get through.
I could not get Sir Henry Thornton to agree to any compromise. I pleaded with him, but he refused. The directors appealed to me. They said they could not bring about economies because he opposed them. Finally, after the discussions-I want to be careful of my words-before the committee which brought out many extravagances, Sir Henry Thornton came into my office and told me he wanted to offer his resignation to me; after talking it over, he asked me if I would agree to his getting a bonus of some kind- I forget the exact word-when he resigned, and I said I would. We gave him altogether over $100,000; I think it was S125,000. He had Britton Osier, a lawyer from Toronto, working for him, and it took about a month. Finally we gave him, I think, about $125,000; at any rate it was over $100,000. At no time did Sir Henry Thornton and I have words about it.
I simply say, Mr. Speaker, that the $19,000,000 that I have shown of economies between 1931 and 1937 were justification to us for the pressure we put on the Canadian National Railways for economies. It was justification for my pressing Sir Henry Thornton to agree to economies. If Sir Henry Thornton had agreed to economies at headquarters -which had nothing to do with the men-I admit frankly, he would never have reached the stage of putting in his resignation or had any difficulty whatsoever. He and I were good friends, and before I sit down I take the liberty of quoting him. Here is his statement taken from the Canadian National Magazine. Sir Henry Thornton, as president of the road, was speaking of the Minister of Railways of that time-myself. Sir Henry said:
I should like to take this opportunity of saying that I have served under a number of

The Address-Mr. Dunning
ministers of the crown, but I have never served under one for whom I had more real affection than for the present incumbent of that post.
We have in him one who ardently desires the welfare of the Canadian National Railways system, one whose heart beats with ours and one who, in addition to the performance of his ministerial duties, is likewise a really fine friend.
Perhaps it is not modest of me to quote it, but I think it is only fair to do so because of the charges that have been made against me.
Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker, and I have presented them as honestly as I know how. If, after this, statements are made to contradict them, all I have to say is that if they are made by members of this house, at any rate they will be stating what they know to be not true.
In regard to the subamendment submitted by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, which will be voted on shortly, I have only a word or two to say. Let me first read it:
That the amendment be amended by adding the following thereto: "We are of the opinion that these conditions can be remedied only by the effective control of financial institutions^ and monopolistic enterprises which are exploiting the Canadian people."
Whether accidentally or intentionally, and I imagine accidentally, the language of the amendment is confusing. It says:
We are of the opinion that these conditions can be remedied only by the effective control of financial institutions-
That is part of it. Then it goes on, in the same sentence, it is true:
-and monopolistic enterprises which are exploiting the Canadian people.
If they had said that conditions could be remedied by the effective control of monopolistic enterprises, I think the whole house could agree with the sentiment behind that; but when they say "effective control of financial institutions," I do not think the language expresses their thought. Anyway it does not express mine, and so far as I am concerned I am not going to support it.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Yes.

Is there a comma
after "financial institutions"?

Not in this copy I am
reading from.
Therefore does not the modifying clause modify both "financial institutions" and "monopolistic enterprises"?

Whether the comma is in or out, and I do not think it makes any particular difference, I think the subamendment is badly worded. I do not think it is the thought of the hon. gentleman who moved it. If it is, at all events it is not my thought. ' I cannot support it anyway. I am naturally going to support my own amendment.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I am moved to address you very briefly because of the fact, as stated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) this evening, that it was my good or ill fortune to be Minister of Railways for Canada during the period of greatest expansion of the Canadian National railway system.
My hon. friend has pointed out that during that period the investments of the Canadian people in the Canadian National Railways grew very rapidly. That is correct. What he did not point out was that during that period the revenues of the Canadian National Railways grew very much more rapidly.
When my hon. friend spoke of the addition of interest charges during the period from 1925 to 1930, he omitted to state that the ability of the railway company to carry interest charges grew during that period to such a point that for the only two years in the history of the system we had a net return over and above the amount required to pay the interest. This does not mean that I think my judgment, or the judgment of the management of the Canadian National Railways, or the judgment of the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway, or the judgment of nearly all the industrialists and financiers of Canada, was quite accurate during that period as to what was coming four or five years later. Is it any disgrace to admit it? Hon. gentlemen who were members of this house during that period will remember my experience of coming here as Minister of Railways to propose the building of branch lines, and what was the response of the house, and particularly the response of hon. gentlemen opposite? Always demanding more and more, year after year.
I do not remember that I ever did, but I am not going to quarrel with my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was the attitude of the opposition. The then member for Inverness comes to my mind, and others would come to mind if I were not speaking extemporaneously.
In respect to the taking over of defunct railway lines, during the period for which
The Address-Mr. Dunning

I was responsible as minister we took over the Gaspe railway line. Will any member of this house rise in his place to-day and say that the Gaspe line should not be a part of the Canadian National railway system? During my period as Minister of Railways we also took over the Inverness railway. Will any member rise in his place and say that the Inverness railway should not to-day be part of the Canadian National railway system?
Better not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
During the same period hon. members, the Alberta members, will remember the great competition which was developing between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National with respect to getting into northern Alberta with their respective lines. They will remember the pressure that I as minister endeavoured to exert to prevent useless duplication by the two railways, and the two of them jointly bought out the railway lines then owned by the government of Alberta. Will any hon. member to-day say that the Northern Alberta railway should not be a part of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways? I am sure he will not.
And there, Mr. Speaker, is a complete list of the so-called defunct railways with the exception of the Quebec Southern from Montreal northwards; and in that connection may I say that there was no political pressure from any quarter with respect to it. Time after time during three years Sir Henry Thornton pleaded with me to agree to and to recommend to the government the taking over of that road because of the advantages, demonstrated by his technical men in great detail, which it was supposed would come from it.

May I interrupt my hon. friend? I do not wish to bother him; but I have looked over that file, and not only was there political pressure but I can name one of his colleagues who used it and who is sitting within a few feet of him now. Sir Henry Thornton opposed it over and over again, and finally accepted under political pressure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, if there were political pressure on Sir Henry Thornton I was not aware of it. There was none on me. I can only affirm that Sir Henry Thornton during several years urged repeatedly that it be taken over. At any rate I have reduced the defunct railroads to that one. Apparently my hon. friend would say that the Quebec Southern should not be part of the Canadian National Railways.
{Mr. Dunning.]
And that road is a paying proposition to-day.
I do not think any railroad they took over is a paying proposition. None of the three the hon. gentleman has mentioned is, and I am also certain the Quebec Southern is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend can argue that from now until doomsday-
We know now who was the minister who put the political pressure on the hon. gentleman to take it over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We can argue from now until doomsday whether a particular piece of the Canadian National Railways is or is not a paying proposition. But, as was put to me in the house many times by hon. gentlemen on the other side, there was with respect to these matters, branch and other lines, an obligation on parliament to serve the Canadian people with equipped transportation facilities, and never was it expressed more strongly; never was I subjected to more criticism. My hon. friend speaks with some heat -and I can understand it-of accusations against himself of sabotaging-I think was the word-the Canadian National Railways; but does he not remember how all across this country it was published during the years 1927 and 1928 that I, because of alleged friendship with the Canadian Pacific Railway, was hindering Sir Henry Thornton's great scheme of expansion of the people's system.
I never said it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Probably not, but my hon. friend's friends did, and the press which supported his party did. I went through that experience, Mr. Speaker. That is one of the things which is inseparable from government ownership and the discussion of a government-owned enterprise in a democratic assembly. We have to take it whether we like it or not. Whether we are here or hon. gentlemen opposite are here, the people's representatives will speak their minds and the minds of their people, will give vent to the suspicions which they entertain, and all our complaining in that regard will not make a bit of difference.
Let me make just one observation with regard to political promises. I know my hon. friend will forgive me for reminding him of some of his own. I am sure he remembers going to Manitoba. I am sure he remembers categorically promising that if his party were returned to power in 1930, the Mafeking cut-off would be built.

The Address-Mr. Church
Mr. Speaker, I absolutely deny that I ever made any such promise. I admit the promise was made in that election, but I never made any such promise.
My hon. friend made it in his address in the town of Dauphin during the election in 1930.

I made no such promise; I make the statement again. Just because a couple of ministers over there make the statement that I made that promise does not prove it. I state that I did not make the promise. I think I ought to know something about my own promises.
If I may be permitted, I was present-
Order.

and I will take my oath that the hon. gentleman who is now leader of the opposition did say, speaking in Dauphin town hall, that if he were returned to power, his party would build the Mafeking cut-off and it would be built forthwith.

Mr. Speaker, I ask the
hon. gentleman who rose in his place and said I made that promise to bring forward the quotation that I made such a statement.
Oh, oh.

No, I am not unfair
enough to ask him to do it now-that is a fancy trick such as we get from hon. gentlemen opposite-but we are just beginning this session; we have plenty of time, and I ask him to bring it forward at the proper time and show me where I made it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now that this Donny-brook is over, may I continue? I merely cited an instance which, whether my hon. friend was guilty or not guilty, was certainly widely published at the time. I called upon my own memory with respect to it and got it confirmed by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) who says he heard it there. We shall, however, allow the hon. member for Dauphin and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) to settle that between themselves. AH I desire to say, Mr. Speaker, is this, and this is the really serious word. The administration of a great public utility demands a degree of restraint on the part of all of us to which none of us in this parliament has so far proved equal. That is my firm belief. No matter which party of us is in opposition, we do belabour the government politically with respect to the administration of this great utility. That has been the 71492-38
history to date. I mention it merely in order that in this time of great difficulty we may all look at it-and I do not except hon. gentlemen in the corner; they are not any more righteous than the rest of us in that regard; I include everybody, including myself. There is no subject about which in the interests of Canda we require more heart searching than in regard to statements we make with respect to the conduct of our great publicly owned utility. That is all I want to say. I have spoken quite extemporaneously, because my hon. friend referred to these matters.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I ask permission to call attention to a remark made in this debate this afternoon with reference to myself by the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair) which I think, when his attention is called to it, he will withdraw. The short statement which the hon. member made at ten minutes to six, when I was not in the house, was that-
. . . one of the hon. members from Toronto said, "I view with alarm the visit of Cordell Hull to Canada." Yes, he viewed with alarm the visit of a friendly ambassador to Canada.
Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East): Who said that?
Mr. Blair:	What is Tommy Church's constituency?	.
Mr. Lapointe: Broadview.
Mr. Blair:	Broadview?-the name is a
misnomer. There is no "broadview" about that -it is one of the narrowest things I ever heard, in regard to Americans. And we are at war with them, because Cordell Hull comes to visit us! There are views of things which I wish, for the sake of civilization and for the sake of common decency and courtesy, could be erased from Hansard.
Mr. Speaker, I never on any occasion made remarks like that. I have too much respect for the famous statesman who was visiting the university of Toronto to receive a degree. Also, I have welcomed and received thousands and tens of thousands of Americans and conventions as I lived in a city near '-hr border, and this is the first time in all these long years I have been in the public service that it has been suggested that a discourteous remark of that kind had been made by me about any of them. May I say to the hon. member that he did not have a newspaper in his hand nor did he read from one. He never read such an article, and no newspaper ever published such an article. What I did say was this, after referring to the very fine reception at the university accorded to a distinguished and honoured United States citizen: I said that I viewed with alarm the

The Address-Mr. Church

effect which I believed the Anglo-American treaty would have on empire preferences, on the Ottawa agreements, and on acute unemployment in Toronto. No reference was made in that connection to the distinguished statesman the hon. member mentioned: Mr. Cordell Hull. He has not the paper, cannot produce it, and never saw any such statement in any paper. I have too high a regard for that distinguished statesman and for the American people to make such an absurd statement anywhere. I have welcomed tens of thousands of American visitors at conventions in a long public career, and never on any occasion have I shown any discourtesy to or any disrespect for the great nation which they represented and which I hold in the highest regard. If the hon. gentleman will say the same thing outside the house to-morrow, I will immediately sue him for libel and slander. He never saw such a statement in any paper, and his memory is not correct.
I simply gave a report which I saw in a paper. The hon. gentleman says he did not say it, and I accept his word and apologize.

Would my hon. friend
have any objection to the house proceeding to government notices of motion so that we might introduce the three resolutions under that heading?
JMr. Martin.]

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: To-night?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
I think we have been here long enough.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would take only about two minutes, but if there is objection to introducing them I would move that the house do now adjourn.

What will be the business
to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
To-morrow
we shall take whatever business appears on the order paper. We shall start at the beginning and go right on, just in the order in which it appears.

I assume the government
will introduce the three government orders to which the Prime Minister has just referred?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That was what I wanted to do, to take up the three government notices of motion in order that we might be in a position to bring them on to-morrow. All that is necessary is for the house to permit the ministers to state that His Excellency the Governor General has been informed of the subject matter of these resolutions and recommends them to the house. Then tomorrow they would appear under government orders, but if we cannot do that they will just stay where they are.

The Minister of Finance
(Mr. Dunning) and I have made long speeches to-night, and I think we need a rest. We had better leave it until to-morrow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Very well.
I move that the house do now adjourn.
